medSchoolStudLife.leaveOfAbsence: Students in good academic standing have the option to take voluntary leave from the school of medicine.  This leave can be designated as either personal or medical leave.   LOA's are approved through the Academic Affairs Office (AAO), in consultation with the Student Affairs Office (SAO), and cannot exceed 12 total months over the course of the student's entire medical school enrollment.  Students may be placed on mandatory medical leave if the AAO and SAO, in consultation with the Dean, determine that the student is endangering him/herself, other university community members or patients by continuation as a medical student.  Students may also be placed on administrative leave by the AAO or the Academic Standards and Professionalism Committee when there are academic or professionalism deficiencies not addressed by other type of leaves.
medSchoolStudLife.organizationActivities: Marshall medical students have the opportunity to become actively involved with a variety of student organizations including the Medical Student Council,  American Medical Student Assn., the American Medical Assn.-Medical Student Section, the American Medical Women's Assn. and many specialty interest groups.  A number of students have been successful in gaining regional, state or national positions of leadership.  The initiation of new organizations is highly supported, such as Phi Delta Epsilon International Medical Fraternity, the Gold Humanism Honor Society and the Student National Medical Association.  Community service activities include the Marshall Medical Outreach program which provides free health care to the homeless population and Dreamcatchers, a network of students who are dedicated to fulfilling the end of life dreams of local hospice patients.
medSchoolStudLife.housing: The Admissions Office maintains a list of apartments and landlords.   There is a Professional and Graduate student residential apartment community located adjacent to the health sciences campus,
medSchoolStudLife.supportSystems: The Marshall University Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine is committed to creating an inclusive and supportive environment for students of all gender identities and sexual orientations. Medical students have access to university-wide LGBTQ+ resources through Marshall University, as well as student organizations and affinity groups that promote advocacy, education, and peer support. The School of Medicine also incorporates training in culturally competent care for LGBTQ+ patients within the curriculum and offers programming focused on diversity, equity, and inclusion. Faculty mentorship, student-led initiatives, and institutional support help ensure that gender and sexual minority students feel welcomed, supported, and empowered throughout their medical education.
medSchoolStudLife.supportSystemsForDisabilities: The Marshall University Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine provides robust support for applicants and learners with disabilities or learning differences. Students have access to university and school-based accessibility services, including individualized academic accommodations, assistive technology, and testing support. Full-time learning specialists, academic advising faculty, and peer tutors work with students to enhance study strategies, test-taking skills, and understanding of course material. Peer mentoring offers new students connections with experienced peers, fostering encouragement and guidance. These layered resources ensure all students can access the curriculum fully and achieve academic and professional success.
medSchoolStudLife.wellnessPrograms:
PROJECT P.R.E.M.E.D. (Providing Real World Experiences to future Marshall Educated Doctors) is a medical school pathway program. Selected students participate in a one-week immersion program exposing them to life as a medical student. Participants take part in various interactive workshops and learning sessions with JCESOM faculty, residents and medical students. Most importantly, participants leave the program with an assigned medical student mentor who assists them on their pathway to medical school. 

STUDENT NATIONAL MEDICAL ASSOCIATION is committed to "supporting current and future underrepresented medical students”, addressing the needs of under-served communities and increasing the number of clinically excellent, culturally competent and socially conscious physicians.

PREMEDICAL MENTORING ADVISING PROGRAM (PMAP) was designed to prepare undergraduate students for admission to medical school. 

HEALTH SPECTRUM ALLIANCE (HSA) is the medical-student run, student organization whose mission is to cultivate - through activism, education, and membership - an environment of safety and pride for past, current, and future students, faculty and staff. Building support both on and off campus, HSA Strives to break down biases and barriers within the medical school community to further combat inequalities facing both physicians and patients. Membership is free and open to students from all Marshall University Health Science Schools and all are welcome.

WellHerdMD - a wellness program that offers a variety of activities and resources to help medical students achieve and maintain optimal health.  This includes mental health counseling, physical fitness programs, professional coaching to develop healthy habits and manage stress, education workshops, and other resources.   See website for more information. 
 https://jcesom.marshall.edu/students/wellherd-md-student-wellness-program
medSchoolStudLife.campusCulture: The campus culture at the Marshall University Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine is collaborative, supportive, and mission-driven. Students learn in a close-knit environment where faculty are approachable and mentorship is strongly emphasized. The school fosters teamwork rather than competition, encouraging students to support one another throughout their training. With a strong focus on service to Appalachia, students are actively engaged in community outreach, rural health initiatives, and early clinical experiences. Located in Huntington, the medical school is part of a welcoming community that values its learners and provides a balanced environment for both professional development and personal well-being.
medSchoolStudLife.transportationAdditionalInfo: There will be times during the pre-clinical and clinical clerkships years will travel from the main medical school campus to the Huntington VA Medical Center campus, St. Mary's Medical Center and other site-specific assignments.

medSchoolCurriculum.tutoringPrograms: Students have options to work with individual faculty, course directors, mentors, peer tutors, learning specialists, and the support staff of the Office of Student Affairs and Academic Support.
medSchoolCurriculum.patientInteraction: Students begin patient interactions during the second semester of the first year and also receive significant patient contact during their third year in each of the seven clinical rotations.
medSchoolCurriculum.instructionStyle: A blend of pedagogies, including independent and team-based learning, simulations, standardized patient encounters, workshops, case discussions, lectures, and labs, maximizes student learning.
medSchoolCurriculum.clinicalRotations: In the third year, our students take seven distinct rotations, which eight weeks each, including Pediatrics, Surgery, Internal Medicine, Family Medicine, Ob/Gyn, Neurology/Psychiatry.
medSchoolCurriculum.lectureAttendance: Lecture attendance is not mandatory; however,  most other forms of teaching. such as group learning and laboratories. are required.
medSchoolCurriculum.curricularHighlights:
The School of Medicine offers an integrated systems-based curriculum that consists of nine integrated courses in years one and two. The year one courses include Physicians in Practice, Molecular and Cellular Foundations of Disease, Microbiology and Host Defense, Hematology and Oncology, The Musculoskeletal System, and Neural Networks. Year two courses cover Nutrition, Gastroenterology, Cardiology, Nephrology, Pulmonology, Reproductive Health, and the Endocrine System. Longitudinal clinical skills courses, Patient Care and Clinical Skills, are integral parts of year 1 and 2 where students learn and hone their early clinical skills.
Year 3 comprises of six, eight-week rotations in clinical subspecialties, including pediatrics, internal medicine, family medicine, surgery/orthopedics, obstetrics and gynecology, and neurology (4-weeks) and psychiatry (4-weeks).
Year 4 includes required rotations in emergency medicine, sub–internship and ICU, and 36 weeks of unstructured time for research and career electives and/or away rotations.
medSchoolCurriculum.primaryCarePrograms: The Family Medicine, Pediatrics and Internal Medicine Departments all have student interest groups that meet throughout the year and give presentations about their specialty to the medical students. All three departments provide didactic lectures in the second and third years of the curriculum on primary care topics as well. Our third- and fourth-year curriculum is designed to give students exposure to primary care fields. A number of our students also chose rural experiences that further exposes them to primary care in smaller communities.
medSchoolCurriculum.researchPrograms: The Office of Research and Graduate Education awards MS (Research or Medical Sciences), MS (Clinical & Translational Science), Ph.D., B.S./Ph.D and combined M.D./Ph.D. degrees. Our research programs use both biomedical and translational approaches to address the prevalent health disparities in West Virginia and Appalachia. Clinical outcomes and translational research infrastructure including instructional clinics in Biostatistics and Research Design, Institutional Review Board (IRB), Institutional Animal Care and Use, and Scholarly Activities are available through the Department of Clinical and Translational Science, located in the Translational Genomic Research Institute. Pilot research funding is available through the Appalachian Clinical and Translational Sciences Institute, Appalachian Center for Cellular Transport in Obesity Related Disorders, and Center for Rural Health. All MS1 students can receive a research stipend for a summer research project between MS1 and MS2 years.
medSchoolCurriculum.academicSystemText: The pedagogy is mixed with special emphasis on skill-development, professionalism, and communication competencies.
medSchoolCurriculum.communityServiceText: Although not required, community service is emphasized and our students participate fully in our Marshall Medical Outreach, the Honduras medical trip and other community service projects annually.
medSchoolCurriculum.researchThesisText: Students participate in bench, educational, or clinical research.  Research is offered throughout the MD curriculum, especially during the summer of year two and up to 12 weeks in year four.

medSchoolInformation.generalInformation: The Marshall University Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine was granted full accreditation and graduated its first class in 1981. The School of Medicine is a community-based program which provides learning opportunities in varied settings: a state-of-the-art ambulatory care center, the Veterans Affairs Medical Center, rural clinics, highly specialized tertiary-care hospitals, offices of private physicians and others.  Educational opportunities are further enhanced by the Edwards Comprehensive Cancer Center, the Robert C. Byrd Biotechnology Science Center and the Byrd Clinical Center.
medSchoolInformation.missionStatement: The Marshall University Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine is a community-based, Veterans Affairs affiliated medical school dedicated to providing high quality medical education and postgraduate training programs to foster a skilled physician workforce to meet the unique healthcare needs of West Virginia and Central Appalachia. Building upon its medical education foundation, the school seeks to develop centers of excellence in clinical care, including primary care in rural underserved areas as well as focused and responsive programs of biomedical science graduate study, biomedical and clinical science research, academic scholarship and public service outreach. The School is committed to fulfilling its mission by creating a diverse and inclusive academic community that is sustained in a collegial and nurturing environment of life-long learning.

medSchoolApplication.typicalInterviewDay:
PROBABLE INTERVIEW FORMAT FOR 2026 ENTERING CLASS
•	Applicants invited to interview participate in a live virtual interview conducted via a secure platform (e.g., Zoom/Teams) scheduled by the Admissions Office.

You’ll enter a waiting room and then be placed into a breakout room with two interviewers. They alternate asking questions.

The interview typically lasts around 40–45 minutes.

After the interview portion, you return to the main session while the interviewers discuss your responses. Admissions staff then conclude with a brief wrap‑up and outline next steps.

Applicants must attend a student session (virtual) within two weeks of the interview; a virtual faculty session is optional but recommended.

Interview Requirements:

All interviewees are required to complete and submit an Interview Agreement and provide a valid photo ID before the start of their interview.

medSchoolApplication.additionalInfo:
**Response to COVID-19 - Information for 2026 Admissions Cycle** 
Please note the following information regarding coursework, labs and letters of evaluation: 
 
•	Pass/Fail Coursework –We will accept Pass/Fail and CR/NC grading for prerequisite coursework for Spring Semester 2020 only. 
 
•	Online Coursework and Labs - Courses and labs delivered via remote learning due to COVID-19 will be accepted for Spring 2020 through Spring 2022 terms. All courses taken AFTER Spring 2022 must be in-person and letter graded.  

•	Letters of Recommendation – A Premedical Advisory Committee letter or three letters of recommendation from individuals who can speak to the applicant's qualifications for entering the field of medicine are required.  We participate in the AMCAS Letter Service and receive letters electronically.   All letters must be submitted through AMCAS by December 15 of the year prior to matriculation.   Additional pertinent letters of recommendation are welcome but are not required. 

•	MCAT – The MCAT is required and must be taken within three calendar years prior to matriculation.  

Qualified Applicants can apply regardless of their state of legal residence.  As a state assisted medical school Marshall gives preference to its state residents.  All applicants must be U.S. Citizens or hold a permanent resident visa.

medSchoolApplication.courseworkAcceptanceInfo:
Medical schools choose to accept community college courses for several compelling reasons. 

Community colleges also serve as a valuable resource for high school students seeking to earn academic or dual credit before graduation. This approach not only expedites their undergraduate education but also positions them to potentially enter medical school earlier, courtesy of college credits accrued during high school. Furthermore, community colleges offer a financially prudent alternative for post-high school students. Many individuals face financial constraints that hinder them from enrolling in a four-year institution away from home. By enrolling in community college courses for a year or two, students can significantly reduce tuition and fees, while living at home allows for additional savings to support their remaining college education.

Lastly, community college courses often accommodate non-traditional applicants, such as those who are employed or juggling other responsibilities. The availability of late afternoon and evening classes means that potential applicants can complete the required in person prerequisites  for medical school without having to resign from their jobs, thereby broadening access to medical education for a more diverse range of applicants.

medSchoolApplication.technicalStandardInfo:
Technical Standards for Medical School

To matriculate, progress, and graduate, students at the Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine must meet essential abilities and qualities necessary for safe, effective, and ethical patient care.

Key Areas:

Observation & Communication: Accurately gather and convey information from patients and colleagues.

Motor & Sensory Skills: Perform physical exams, procedures, and use medical instruments safely.

Cognitive Abilities: Think critically, solve problems, and integrate information quickly.

Behavioral & Social Attributes: Demonstrate professionalism, emotional stability, and teamwork.

Ethics & Professionalism: Uphold ethical standards, integrity, and lifelong learning.

Students who cannot meet these standards, with or without reasonable accommodations, may be unable to complete the curriculum. The School considers accommodations on a case-by-case basis in accordance with federal regulations.

The medical school's supplemental application fee will be waived for individuals who have been granted an AMCAS fee waiver. medSchoolSelection.premedReqRec:
Entrants should have a bachelors degree from an accredited college or university.  Prerequisites must be completed with a grade of "C" or better at an accredited US or Canadian college or university. Science prerequisites may not be taken online.  

Minimum course requirements are: 
General biology or zoology (with lab) -  8 semester hours
General chemistry (with lab) - 8 semester hours 
Organic chemistry (with lab)  - 8 semester hours 
Biochemistry - 3 semester hours
Physics (with lab) - 8 semester hours
English - 6 semester hours
Social or behavioral - 6 semester hours
Statistics/Biostatistics (3 semester hours) - 

Highly recommended courses:  Cell and Molecular Biology (3 semester hours); 300 or higher level Anatomy course  (3 semester hours); 300 or higher level Physiology course (3 semester hours).
medSchoolSelection.selectionFactors: There is no discrimination because of race, gender, religion, age, disability, sexual orientation, or national origin.  The MCAT is required and must be taken within three calendar years of matriculation.  Applicants are evaluated and selected who demonstrate an exceptional balance of experiences and attributes that are most in-line with the school's mission.    As a state-assisted institution, preference is given to WV residents.  Qualified nonresident applicants will also be considered.  For the most up-to-date selection factors see: https://jcesom.marshall.edu/admissions/admissions-criteria/ .
medSchoolSelection.preMedShadowText: Premedical shadowin is highly recommended to assure the applicant that medicine is their correct career choice.    Community services also highly valued.
